I have several years of programming experience and currently work on real-world projects. I enjoy turning ideas into working products, problem-solving, and presenting projects clearly. summary: OUT OF REACH is a first-person space-survival game in which the mission you design is the mission you must survive. At the launch pad you physically load the cargo for AURORA-7, a fictional Mars research ship, against a 60-second deadline and real engineering limits: a 600 kg payload, an 800-credit budget, electrical power and supplies for 30 crew-days. Science or safety margin? Every crate is a trade-off. Later, deep in space, a debris strike cripples power, life support and the antenna, and every repair, spacewalk and meal is paid for with what you packed. NASA/JPL Horizons distances set the radio delay, so no answer from Earth arrives faster than light, and NASA life-support baseline values drive oxygen, CO2, water and food. Across 30 compressed days you eat, sleep, decide and wait for a rescue that is never instant. A mission record then explains why you lived or died, so players without aerospace training feel the trade-offs mission designers face.
details: Playable Windows build, 30-second demo video, 7-slide deck, README and credits: https://github.com/alex-slovakia/out-of-reach/releases WHAT IT DOES OUT OF REACH is a first-person space-survival game in which the mission you design is the mission you must survive. You are Houston, the only crew member of AURORA-7, a fictional research ship bound for Mars. 1. Design: at launch complex LC-7 you carry crates onto the transport within real limits (600 kg payload, 800 credits, power load versus generation, supplies for 30 crew-days) in 60 seconds. A science load carries a 90 kg spectrometer and exactly the spare parts the repairs will need; a redundancy load trades science for battery, oxygen and parts. 2. Launch with a real NASA countdown on the radio, then later, deep in space, a debris strike: power 20 percent, life support and antenna down, CO2 rising. 3. Repair with the parts and energy you packed. Every prompt shows the exact cost; a refused action spends nothing. 4. Spacewalk to the antenna: preparation, airlock, tether rope, a 3-hour suit oxygen supply. 5. Call Earth once from a terminal that shows a real NASA EPIC photograph of Earth. On day 1 Earth is 197,707,976 km away, so no reply can arrive before 31 min 59 s of mission time (still over 30 minutes on day 9); reserves drain while you wait. 6. Survive 30 days in chapters (days 1, 5, 9, 14, 20, 30): meals, sleep in the berth, ordinary days as a short montage, hard choices, a day-14 announcement on your handheld radio delayed by real light time, and a rescue window you must power. 7. A rescue craft docks before your eyes under NASA's Deep Star Maps sky, or the loss is stated with its cause. A mission record explains why; restart with a different design. WHAT PLAYERS LEARN Mass, power, money and consumables compete. Communication is limited by light speed. Life support is several separate jobs: with scrubbers down, CO2 reaches the ISS emergency level in about 20.5 hours, long before the oxygen runs out. Spacewalks cost time, oxygen and risk. Time itself is a consumable. HOW IT WORKS A deterministic C# simulation owns one mission clock and one resource ledger in real units; spending is all-or-nothing. An offline NASA/JPL Horizons snapshot (32 daily Earth-Mars vectors, SHA-256 checked) gives distance / speed of light, both ways, plus 600 s of assumed processing; the range and the one-way delay stay on screen during play, together with the Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra) that has Mars above its horizon. NASA BVAD rates (0.84 kg O2, 1.01 kg CO2, 2.5 kg water, 1.83 kg food per crew-day) drive consumption; cabin CO2 uses the ideal gas law; spacewalk costs follow BVAD EVA values. A radiation line estimates the dose from NASA's MSL RAD cruise measurement (1.8 mSv per day), for information only. Time compression is always shown; the routine montage never skips a danger. AURORA-7, its position proxy, the rescue and the prices are labelled fiction. All 544 automated EditMode tests and 178 PlayMode scene tests pass on the submitted build, plus human playtests. WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE A complete half-hour mission that students can lose for an understandable reason and replay with a better design; next, team play for up to four roles, new destinations, a launch-date picker with fresh Horizons data and teacher notes. TOOLS Unity 6000.3.28f1 (URP), C#, Windows x64; Blender and Python for original 3D models; NumPy, Pillow, FFmpeg, Git LFS. AI coding assistants Claude Code and OpenAI Codex wrote code, procedural assets and documentation under our direction; all dialogue voices are synthetic (Google Gemini text-to-speech). Third-party assets are credited in the references and on the in-game Sources page. The spacecraft and mission are fictional; no NASA endorsement is implied.
